content: Trained and supervised community health workers are capable of dispensing antiretroviral therapy (ART) between regular clinical visits. This recommendation is strongly supported by moderate-quality evidence. It applies to all adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV. The availability of health workers remains insufficient in many high HIV-burden settings. Task shifting and task sharing involve redistributing responsibilities within healthcare teams. Specific tasks are reassigned to health workers with shorter training and fewer qualifications to optimize human resources. While increasing the number of healthcare personnel is essential, sharing and shifting clinical tasks ensures adequate workforce availability. In 2013, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued recommendations on task shifting for initiating, maintaining, and dispensing ART. These recommendations are based on a systematic review of four randomized controlled trials and six observational studies. The data showed no difference in mortality and some evidence of reduced loss to follow-up rates when nurses or non-physician clinicians initiated or maintained ART, or when community health workers maintained ART, compared to physicians performing these tasks. The quality of care in these studies was ensured through training, mentoring, supervision, clear referral pathways, and effective monitoring and evaluation systems. New guidelines recommend that trained and supervised lay providers distribute ART to adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV. Many high HIV-burden settings face critical shortages of pharmacy personnel, particularly in rural and primary-care settings. Community distribution of ART for stable individuals can reduce the burden on health services and patients by decreasing the frequency of clinical consultations and drug pick-up visits. Retrospective cohort studies from Uganda, Tanzania, and Zambia show that community ART distribution results in significantly lower patient attrition compared to facility-based services. Indirect evidence from a systematic review comparing ART dispensing by non-pharmacists versus pharmacists identified two cluster randomized trials. These trials compared community-based HIV care with clinic-based care. The first trial evaluated patient outcomes, such as viral load, CD4 count, opportunistic infections, and ART regimen changes, when ART was provided in community settings by trained community care counselors living with HIV versus clinic-based ART delivery by health professionals. In community-based settings, ART was distributed by trained and mentored community care counselors who triaged patients, referred them when necessary, and distributed prefilled ART drugs prepared by pharmacy personnel. Patients receiving community-based care had been on ART for more than six months, had no clinical conditions, and reported high adherence to treatment. In the standard-of-care arm, patients visited health facilities monthly, collected ART drugs from facility pharmacies, and received care from health workers. The second trial evaluated virological failure among those accessing ART from lay providers in the community compared to standard ART care delivered by health professionals at health facilities. A meta-analysis found no difference in mortality or virological failure between community-based care and facility-based care. Fewer patients were lost to follow-up in the community-based care group. Both groups demonstrated high levels of self-reported medication adherence, with no statistical differences between them. However, the overall quality of evidence is low. Lay providers were part of broader community-based interventions, which contributed to the success of the approach beyond just ART distribution. A strong recommendation was made that trained and supervised lay providers can distribute ART to adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV, despite the low quality of evidence. This recommendation is supported by programmatic experience with trained and supervised community health workers and lay workers performing other tasks within the HIV care continuum. Additionally, examples from the broader health sector show that community health workers with minimal training can provide curative and preventive care in maternal and child health services, malaria diagnosis and treatment, and tuberculosis care. The public health benefits of lay providers distributing ART include increasing the number of providers to address personnel shortages, reducing clinic congestion, and bringing services closer to communities, which supports retention in care. However, where ART drug supply and stock management are unreliable, distributing ART outside health facilities may increase distribution sites and exacerbate stock-outs. Neither of the two studies in the systematic review included people with comorbidities or children. While the recommendation is relevant to these populations, necessary dose adjustments for children can be safely managed during clinic visits, with maintenance treatment provided at the community level. Initial costs for training and implementing community ART distribution may be higher, but studies report substantial cost savings for patients who no longer need to travel to centralized health services. For example, a study in Uganda found that the cost to patients receiving hospital-based care was three times higher than for those receiving home-based care. Task shifting can enhance linkage to care, treatment adherence, and help HIV programs cope with professional health worker shortages. Strengthened relationships between people with HIV and local communities can empower individuals. In Malawi, community members were hired as pharmacy attendants to pre-package and distribute ART drugs, enhancing pharmaceutical services, reducing waiting times, and alleviating health providers’ workloads at facilities. Successful task-shifting programs require initial and ongoing training, mentoring, supportive supervision, and administrative planning. Programs adopting these recommendations must establish systems for routine supportive supervision of health workers, including lay providers. Regulatory frameworks and national policies may need revision to allow new cadres of health workers to perform these tasks. WHO recommends that all health workers, including lay providers, be adequately remunerated, as volunteer-based health services are difficult to sustain. National regulatory bodies, professional associations, and other stakeholders should address the scope of practice, roles, and responsibilities of health workers. Local supply chain systems must account for task-shifting responsibilities and community models of ART delivery to ensure adequate stock. Trained and supervised non-laboratory staff, including laypeople, can perform blood sample collection via finger-prick testing. Expanding finger-prick testing to lay providers will increase access to essential diagnostics and decentralize HIV care. In many settings, trained and supervised lay providers already conduct HIV testing and perform sample collection using the finger-prick method. No harm has been identified from this approach, but a quality assurance system is necessary for effective and safe implementation. As HIV treatment and care have scaled up, in-service training has played a key role in rapidly upgrading healthcare providers’ competencies. All health workers, including community health workers and lay providers, need regular training, mentoring, and supervision to ensure high-quality care and timely implementation of updated national policies. Countries should consider systems for supporting health workers’ continuing education, including clinical mentoring and regular supportive supervision. New technologies, such as computer-based self-learning, distance education, online courses, and phone-based consultation, can supplement classroom training and optimize health workers’ time and resources. Strengthening HIV treatment and care components in pre-service courses for graduating health workers is equally important. Healthcare workers must be equipped to manage HIV as a chronic condition, work in teams, and implement new national guidelines and protocols. Program managers should support policies to recruit, retain, remunerate, and motivate health workers in rural or remote areas, where turnover and attrition are higher than in urban settings. In many countries, people living with HIV, community workers, and volunteers are involved in delivering HIV testing, counseling, care, treatment, and social support services. People with HIV also serve as expert trainers for health workers. Involving people living with HIV in training health workers and delivering services may help overcome HIV-related stigma and discrimination. Research is needed to determine the feasibility and safety of further task shifting to improve access to treatment, including ART initiation and maintenance at the community level, with spaced clinical visits to health facilities. High-quality evidence is lacking for the initiation of second-line ART by trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses. Further research would identify the benefits and harms of implementing this approach in settings with clinician shortages.
